 Hon'Ble Mrs. Justice Rumi Kumari Phukan

 Judgement And Order (Oral)
Heard Mr. K.N. Choudhury, learned senior counsel appearing for and on behalf of the revision petitioner/accused No.2.
Also heard Ms. S. Jahan, the learned Addl. P.P., Assam, representing the State respondent.

2. The present revision petition is preferred against the concurrent findings of the learned trial Court as well as the learned appellate Court, whereby the petitioner/accused No.2 was convicted under Section 16(1)(A-1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for six months and to pay a fine of Rs.5,000/- (rupees five thousands) only, in default simple imprisonment for another three months.

3. The prosecution case in brief is that on 17.06.2005, the Food Inspector of Kamrup visited the premises of M/s. Deepak Store at Barabazar (owner Deepak Dey), Pandu and suspecting to be adulterated, collected 9 bottles of food drink (orange drink of Shaad Brand), containing 180 ml. in each bottle from the total stock of 72 numbers of bottle, imported to India by M/s. Green India,
Karimganj and seized the same in presence of the witnesses.

4. On 18.06.2005, the seized articles were sent to the Public Analyst, Assam for analysis, who in his report dated 28.07.2005 opined that the sample of the food drink (orange drink of Shaad Brand), is misbranded as per the provision of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rule 40 of the PFA Rules, 1955 (as amended) and after getting the necessary prosecution sanction from the Local Health Authority, the Food Inspector filed the offence report before the trial Court against two accused, namely, the vendor Deepak Dey, proprietor of M/s. Deepak Store, as the accused No.1 and M/s. Green India, Karimganj as the accused No.2 (importer), which was registered as CR No.
4302c/2005.

entities.text: Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rule 40
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Page No.# 3/10 5.

On appearance of the accused persons before the learned trial Court, the copies of the offence report along with other documents were furnished to them and considering the materials available on record, charge under Section 16(1)(A-1) of the Act was framed and explained against both accused persons, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.
6. During the course of trial, the prosecution examined two witnesses and recorded the statement of the accused persons under Section 313 of the CrPC.
The defence also examined two witnesses in their support.

7. At the conclusion of the trial, the learned trial Court vide order dated 10.04.2015, sentenced both accused persons including the present accused/petitioner to undergo simple imprisonment for 6 Crl.Rev.P./35/2016 on 12 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46241990/
2 (six) months and to pay a fine of Rs.5,000/- (rupees five thousands) only, in default simple imprisonment for another three months, as stated above.

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and sentence, the petitioner/accused No.2 preferred an appeal before the learned Additional Sessions Judge No. 4, FTC, Kamrup (Metro), vide Criminal Appeal No.33/2015 and the learned appellate Court, by the order dated 10.12.2015, the appeal was dismissed on contest and the conviction and sentence, passed in the C.R. No.4302 C/2005 against the petitioner/accused No.2 was affirmed.
9.

entities.text: Additional Sessions Judge No. 4, FTC, Kamrup (Metro)
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Being aggrieved by both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court, the present revision is preferred by the accused petitioner/accused No.2, on the grounds, inter alia, that the learned Courts below failed to appreciate the evidence on record and the points of law involved in this case, in true perspective and came to a erroneous finding.
Secondly it is contended that the learned trial Court had shifted the burden of proof on the distributor/wholesaler, which is bad in law and as such the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside.

It is further contended that the concerned drinks were brought into India from Bangladesh after proper analysis by the Public Health Laboratory, which certified that the concerned product conforms the standards of food drink and prays for setting aside Page No.# 4/10 the impugned judgment of conviction and sentence and acquit accused petitioner from the said offence.
10. Heard the submission of Mr. K.N. Choudhury, learned senior counsel appearing for and on behalf of the accused/petitioner.
Also heard Ms. S. Jahan, the learned Addl. P.P., Assam for the State respondent.
11. I have carefully gone through the record of the trial Court as well as the appellate and the impugned judgment and order.

12. Be it mentioned that the two accused persons faced the trial for the offence under Section 7 (16)
of the PFA Act.

The vendor Deepak Roy is the accused No. 1, from whose premises, namely, M/s Deepak Store, 9 bottles of food drink (orange drink-shaad brand) were seized, out of the total stock of 72 nos. of the bottles.
As the bottles containing the name of the importer, namely, M/s Green India, Karimganj, so the offence report was submitted against both the accused persons and both of them stood the trial.
The plea of the vendor was different than that of the importer and the learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court has dealt with the matter accordingly.

So far as the plea of the vendor is concerned, he sought protection under Section 19 (2) of the PFA Act that as he has purchased the article from the distributor and sold it on the same condition, so he is well protected under the Act.

The vendor also took another plea of violation of Section 10 (7) for not examining the independent witnesses and non-compliance of Section 13 (2), regarding service of notice about the report of Public Analyst.

The learned trial Court, however, rejected all above pleas and convicted him on the basis of Public Analyst Report, which reveals that the sample collected from the shop premises of the vendor was found to be misbranded.

13. So far as regards the present accused petitioner, the learned trial Court did not consider the plea that they imported the article with proper documentation from Bangladesh and it was sold to Crl.Rev.P./35/2016 on 12 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46241990/
3 distributor and wholeseller etc. and no misbranding has been done on their part.

The learned trial Page No.# 5/10 Court also ignored evidence produced by the present accused petitioner No. 2, vide Exhibit- A to I, whereby defence has proved that the food articles were imported from Bangladesh under proper documentation and there is report of the Public Health Laboratory that the food product conforms to the standard.

The trial Court primarily on the basis of the evidence of the Food Inspector/ PW-1, held that the product was imported by M/s Green India, as there was label in the article, they are guilty for selling such article, which was found misbranded by the Public Analyst.

14. On the other hand, the learned appellate Court has given due consideration to the defence evidence produced by the accused petitioner No. 2 and also appreciated the evidence adduced by the prosecution as well as the defence side.

In the impugned judgment, the appellate Court has noted that the accused vendor, Deepak Dey, in his evidence has stated that he purchased the food drink from the hawker through receipt, vide Exhibit-A and he has no knowledge about misbranding.
In that view of the matter, it can be held that the accused No. 1 did not purchase the same from accused No. 2 or its distributor but from hawker.
It is also noted by the appellate Court that M/s Green India denied the sale of product to the accused No. 1/vendor.

The evidence adduced by the present accused petitioner also discussed that they have purchased the food product from Bangladesh and sold the same to different distributors and the accused petitioner also asserted the same aspect in his statement under Section 313 CrPC that he got the article in due manner from Bangladesh and after examination of the seal on the packets, customs authority sent the same for testing at Public Health Laboratory and the Customs Officer gave report, thereby allowing them to sell the product.
All relevant documents have also been proved, vide - Exhibits- A to I and he sold the product in sealed condition in the same state as he received.

The relevant observation of the learned appellate Court is reproduced below:-
"In the present case, it is seen that accused No. 2, M/s Green India in his statement under Section 313 CrPC, asserts that he got the articles in due manner from Bangladesh and after examination of the seal of the packets, Custom authority has sent the articles for testing Page No.# 6/10 at Public Health Laboratory, Guwahati and on the said report, Customs Officer allowed him to sell the product.
During evidence, DW-1 has proved his case through document, Exhibit - A to Exhibit - I.
He asserts that he sold the product in sealed condition in same state as he received and he has no knowledge about the adulteration or misbrand.
After perusal of the documents it is seen that the importer complied with the relevant procedure for importing the articles of food.

Exhibit-D proved by the defence reflects that M/s Green India was allowed for marketing the edible product Litchi drink and Mango drink under brand name "Shaad" imported from Bangladesh through Sutarkandi and Bill of Entry No. is 80/INB/SKD/2005-2006 dated 04.06.2005.

The letter specifically mentioned that the food samples of the said Bill of Entry was sent for chemical analysis to State Public Health Laboratory, Guwahati and same was found to conform to the standard as food drink as per the PFA Rules.
Along with the letter, Exhibit-D, the report of the Public Analyst of the Govt. of Assam has been forwarded and proved.

I, therefore, find that being an importer M/s Green India Crl.Rev.P./35/2016 on 12 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46241990/
4 stored the product of orange drink for marketing only after the Public Analyst of the Govt. of Assam confirmed that the drink conform to the standard of food drink as per provision of PFA Rules at the time of import and only after that, said firm was granted the permission to market the same.
Thus, in my considered opinion, the accused No. 2 cannot be held liable for importing the misbranded food articles as per the provision of Section 5 of the PFA Act.
But in the present case, the allegation against accused is also for distributing/selling of misbranding of the sample orange drink "Shaad" violating Section 40 of the PFA Rules.
The plea of the accused No. 2 is that he distributed the said drinks in same state as he received.

According to Section 14 of the PFA Act, no manufacturer or distributor of, or dealer in, any article of food shall sell such articles to any vendor unless he also gives a warranty in writing in the prescribed form about the nature and quality of each article to the vendor."
Page No.# 7/10 15.

The learned appellate Court in the concluding part of the Judgment has stated that as the label on the sample bottle contained the name of the importer/accused No. 2, which is found to be misbranded, as per the report of the Public Analyst, so he will not be entitled to the benefit of Section 19 (2) of the PFA Act, because there is possibility that the accused No. 2 can also misbrand the said article, before those were distributed and confirmed the conviction given by the trial Court.

16. The learned Senior counsel for the petitioner, Mr K N Choudhury, has vehemently attacked such finding of the appellate Court that despite the learned appellate Court gave a finding that the accused petitioner No. 2 has duly imported the sample as per the documentary evidence and he was permitted to sell the same by the custom also and there is a finding that the accused No. 1 did not purchase the article from the accused No. 2 and the accused petitioner cannot be convicted only because of the label attached to the sample bottle, sold by the vendor, bear the name of importer/petitioner No. 2.
17.
Also heard the submissions of learned Additional Public Prosecutor, who has fairly submitted that one cannot be convicted merely on possibility that he may have misbranded the sample food- product.

It has also been submitted that the protection under Section 19 (2) of the PFA Act is only available to the vendor, but the learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court has held both the accused vendor as well as the importer guilty for violation of Section 19 (2) of the PFA Act.
18.

After going through the record of the trial Court as well as the appellate Court, it is to be noted that the accused petitioner No. 2 has duly produced and proved all the necessary documents that the food drinks were duly purchased from Bangladesh and same was duly tested in the Public Health Laboratory, Government of Assam, Guwahati and such articles were sold thereafter through distributors, dealers etc., but he never sold the sample article to the vendor.

entities.text: Public Health Laboratory, Government of Assam, Guwahati
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text:
Thus, the defence has discharged its duty by giving proper evidence and whereas, vendor also admitted that he purchased the same from the hawker and not from the accused petitioner No. 2, M/s Green India and hence,
Crl.Rev.P./35/2016 on 12 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46241990/
5 there is no proper evidence to connect the present petitioner for sale of said article, by the vendor Page No.# 8/10 from his premises.
The learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court, merely because, no distributor was examined, has held the petitioner guilty, which appears to be not proper.
Although the appellate Court properly appreciated defence evidence, but came to a conclusion contrary to what he has held.

It is also the settled proposition of law that the defence can discharge the burden of proving by preponderance of probability, but not as per the prosecution,
which requires to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.

19. Section 14 of the PFA Act reads as follows:-
"No (manufacturer or distributor or dealer) in any article of food shall sell such article to any such vendor unless he also gives a warranty in writing in the prescribed form about the nature and quality of such article to the vendor.

[Provided that a bill, cash memorandum or invoice in respect of the sale of any article of food given by a manufacturer or distributor of, or dealer in, such article to the vendor thereof shall be deemed to be a warranty given by such manufacturer,
distributor or dealer under this section.]
Explanation- In this section, in sub-section (2) of section 19 and in section 20A, the expression "distributor" shall include a commission agent.]"

20. Obviously, the Section 14 indicates the manufacturer etc. has to give the warranty at the time of selling, but the same is not applicable to the present petitioner being the importer and not the manufacturer.

21. Section 19 reads as follows:-
"19. Defences which may or may not be allowed in prosecutions under this Act.-

(1) It shall be no defence in a prosecution for an offence pertaining to the sale of any adulterated or misbranded article of food to allege merely that the vendor was ignorant of the nature, substance or quality of the food sold by him or that the purchaser having purchased any Page No.# 9/10 article for analysis was not prejudiced by the sale.

(2) A vendor shall not be deemed to have committed an offence pertaining to the sale of any adulterated or misbranded article of food if he proves- (a) that he purchased the article of food- (i) in a case where a licence is prescribed for the sale thereof, from a duly licensed manufacturer, distributor or dealer,
(ii) in any other case, from any manufacturer, distributor or dealer, with a written warranty in the prescribed form; and Crl.Rev.P./35/2016 on 12 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46241990/
6 (b) that the article of food while in his possession was properly stored and that he sold it in the same state as he purchased it.] (3) Any person by whom a warranty as is referred to [in Section 14] is alleged to have been given shall be entitled to appear at the hearing and give evidence."

22. The aforesaid provision relates to the vendor only and not to the manufacturer and/or importer,
but the learned Court has held the accused petitioner guilty under the said provision of law, which is not sustainable.

Only the provision attributable to the importer is Section 5 of the PFA Act, which reads as follows:-
"Section-5- Prohibition of import of certain articles of food- No person shall import into India i) Any adulterated food,
ii) Any misbranded food,
iii) Any article of food for import of which a licence is prescribed, except in accordance of the conditions of licence, and Page No.# 10/10 iv) Any article of food in contravention of any other provision of this Act or any Rule made thereunder."
23.

So far as the present case is concerned, the petitioner is an importer of the articles of food and the article he imported from Bangladesh was tested in the Public Health Laboratory, who certified that the same conforms to standard and Customs gave clearance, which also negate the misbranding on the part of the present petitioner/the importer.
24. In view of the findings and observations made above, this Court is of the opinion that the findings of the Court below is perverse and have crept into illegality.

Accordingly, the impugned order passed by the learned appellate Court, which has affirmed the order of the learned trial Court is hereby quashed and set aside and the accused petitioner is acquitted from the charge and set at liberty forthwith.
25. Revision petition stands allowed.
Return the LCR.
